html:
Harness² Workbench is a web UI, REST API and MCP server that starts processes, holds API keys for cloud models and reads whatever those processes write. It listens on 127.0.0.1 by default, and it is tempting to treat that as a trust boundary. It is not. Any page open in your browser can send requests to localhost. A job the Workbench starts runs as a user on the same machine, and an executor that a model can steer writes the very files the Workbench later reads back to show you results.

So before the repository went public, the code went through two independent security reviews. The reviewer had no part in writing it and started with no prior context. It was given the source and a scratch server, and asked for findings with a working reproduction and a minimal fix. This was an AI security reviewer, not a human penetration test, and the repository says so. The first review, at the end of the build, found 17 issues. The second, a few hours later, checked those fixes, confirmed 12 and judged five partial or acceptable by design, and found 10 more. A final documentation pass found three further code issues, all fixed. Every code fix got a regression test.

This post is what they found, grouped by the lesson behind it.

What held

It is worth starting with the attacks that failed, because they are what a localhost admin tool usually gets wrong:

  • DNS rebinding and cross-site requests. Every request must carry an allowed Host (anything else is a 421), every state-changing request needs a custom header that a cross-site form cannot set, and there is no CORS at all. The second review threw 28 raw-socket cases at the Host, Origin and CSRF checks.
  • Role checks. The first review swept 49 method and path pairs against four roles, the second sent 196 route-and-role requests. No route answered a role it should not.
  • Path traversal in the results reader: encoded .., absolute paths, backslashes, NUL bytes, symlinks and a run directory pointed at /etc.
  • The web UI: hostile content rendered in 21 pages, and 19 ?next= redirect payloads.
  • The egress proxy: 20 server-side request forgery cases, including IP literals, loopback, other ports and credentials in URLs.
  • Fuzzing: 686 hostile requests produced no server error and no panic.

The design choices behind that list (one enforcement point, argv-only process spawning, a strict Content-Security-Policy, no unsafe code) did their job. The findings were somewhere else.

Lesson 1: files a job wrote are hostile input

The largest group of findings came from one fact: a job controls the files the Workbench reads afterwards. Size caps on single files were in place from the start. They were not enough.

Memory amplification. The first review wrote six task summaries of 38 MiB each. One request to list experiments then parsed all of them into JSON trees, and the server's peak memory went from 0.8 GB to 3.8 GB; four requests in parallel reached 14.7 GB. The fix was layered: a 4 MiB cap on a summary, typed parsing that keeps only the fields it needs, a cache keyed on file times, at most four results reads at once, and a per-request budget.

The FIFO swap. The reader checked summary.json with lstat and then opened it. Between the two calls a job can exchange the file with a named pipe in a single renameat2(RENAME_EXCHANGE). A plain open of a FIFO waits for a writer that never comes, while holding one of the four read permits. Do that four times and the results API is dead: the second review's first hang came after about 6 seconds, and by about 35 seconds every results call was timing out, until a restart.

The fix opens every results file with O_NONBLOCK | O_NOFOLLOW and then checks with fstat that the open handle is a regular file with the device and inode lstat saw. Anything else is reported as unreadable and the permit is released. The live check swapped a FIFO over summary.json nine million times while tasks were being listed; no read hung.

Sparse files. The harness fingerprint and the experiment manifest's digest read every file in full, with no cap, because they only computed hashes. A job can create a 1 TiB sparse file that takes no disk space and reads as endless zeroes. Four concurrent harness views over one kept every other results call failing for over a minute; a 64 GiB file took 25.5 seconds. Both readers now record an over-cap file by its size (<too large: N bytes>) without reading it, and refuse more than 64 MiB (fingerprint) or 1 GiB (digest) in total.

Hardlinks defeat per-file caps. Forty sweeps of 63 hardlinked 4 MiB summaries are 9.8 GiB of reading and 4 MiB of disk. A single experiment request ran three threads at full CPU for about eight minutes. The budget is now per request, in bytes and in sweeps; a request that times out or whose client leaves cancels its reads; an experiment lists at most its 200 newest sweeps; and the sweep cache evicts the least recently used entry instead of clearing itself.

Responses grow with their sources, and past them. A 268 MB job log came back as one 268 MB page, and eight concurrent requests took the server from 12.6 MB to 4.2 GB of memory. A 64 MiB harness made of control bytes became a 402 MB JSON response, six times its size, because every byte was escaped. Log pages now stop near 1 MiB and return where to continue. Results responses are built inside their read permit and refused with a 413 above 64 MiB. Job logs themselves have a 256 MiB cap and a free-disk floor, after the first review watched 400 MB of output become a 694 MB log in 29 seconds.

The rule I took away: a reader of untrusted files needs limits on type, size, total, time and concurrency, plus cancellation. Any one of them alone can be walked around.

Lesson 2: an append-only log is a write endpoint

The audit log is a hash chain: each record includes the hash of the previous one, so a later edit breaks the chain. That makes every audited event an endpoint that writes to disk, and the reviews treated it as one.

  • Unauthenticated flooding. Every request with a junk bearer token appended a record. 140,000 such requests added 140,000 records and 33 MB. Failed authentication is now limited to 60 attempts a minute per client (then 429), and at most 10 failures a minute per client are recorded; the rest are only counted in a metric.
  • Authenticated flooding. A viewer token calling an admin-only route 300,000 times in 14 seconds wrote 300,000 records and 90 MB, about 21,000 a second. Refused requests are now recorded at most 10 a minute per principal.
  • The one the documentation pass caught. Refused job starts and cancels were written by the job engine, not the HTTP layer, and the new limit did not cover them: 300 refused requests from an operator token still wrote 300 records. They now share the principal's allowance. Live, 300 refused starts left 10 records, the next 300 refused cancels added none, and an administrator's refusal in the same minute was still recorded.
  • Spoofed actors. A user signed in through the reverse proxy could call themselves initial admin, the name of the bootstrap token, and appear in the log as that token. Actors now carry their kind: token:initial admin and proxy:initial admin are different strings.

The first review also pointed out that the chain is unkeyed: anyone who can write the database can rewrite every record and recompute every hash. That was not fixed in code. The documentation now says plainly that the chain shows edits only by someone who cannot rewrite the data directory, and tells you to record the head hash somewhere else on a schedule.

Lesson 3: identity has to survive proxies and duplicates

  • Repeated proxy headers. In single sign-on mode the Workbench trusted identity headers from a reverse proxy. The first x-forwarded-user won and all x-forwarded-groups values were combined, so a client that added its own x-forwarded-groups: admins became an administrator. A repeated identity header is now a 401, and a repeated Host or Origin header is refused too.
  • A panic before authentication. A login token whose multibyte UTF-8 character straddled byte 8 made the parser's split_at panic. The connection died and the server survived, but an unauthenticated panic is a bug class, not a bug. Tokens are now checked as ASCII first, with a property test over random non-ASCII input.
  • One shared limiter table. Behind a trusted proxy the client address comes from X-Forwarded-For, which any process on the proxy's network can invent. A job filled the 10,000-entry limiter table with made-up addresses in 3.6 seconds, and a real administrator's login from a new address got a 429. Each trusted peer now gets its own share (1,024 clients, then its own overflow bucket), so a peer that floods only limits itself.
  • Long-lived streams. A live-log stream was authorised only when it opened and could run for an hour after its token was revoked. Streams now re-check their credential at every heartbeat. One viewer could also open all 64 stream slots, and 1,100 idle sockets filled the connection limit; both limits are now per principal (8 streams) and per address (256 connections).

Lesson 4: "same machine" means "same user"

The finding with the widest reach (the reviewer rated it medium) was not a bug in the usual sense. In host isolation, harness2's executors run as the Workbench's own user, as they do upstream. The first review's job simply opened the Workbench's database (stored secrets, token hashes) and read /proc/<pid>/environ of the server, which held every secret passed by environment and the proxy shared secret, enough, in single-sign-on mode, to sign in as any user.

What changed:

  • The server and the egress proxy mark themselves non-dumpable at start-up, so a same-user process can no longer read their environment through /proc.
  • The README, the threat model and the setup docs say in bold that a host-mode job is, in effect, a Workbench administrator, and point to container isolation.
  • Container jobs get their variables through a 0600 environment file instead of the runtime command's environment. The profile variables a user may set exclude names that could steer the container runtime or Git (DOCKER_CONTEXT, XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, GIT_SSH_COMMAND and others), after a fake docker script in the review received an attacker's context.
  • Installing harness2 accepts only the commit the release was tested against (unless an administrator opts out), because GitHub serves commits that exist only in forks through the parent repository's URL.
  • Restart recovery used to signal any process group whose leader started late enough, which could hit an unrelated process after a reboot. It now needs the same boot and a job marker in the process's environment.
  • The egress proxy listened on all interfaces by default; it now listens on loopback unless configured otherwise.

What I would do the same way again

Ask for reproductions, not opinions. The resource findings came with numbers: 14.7 GB, 6 seconds, 300,000 records. That made each one impossible to argue with and easy to turn into a regression test.

Review the fixes, not just the code. The second review exists because fixes introduce new attack surface. The per-file caps from the first review were real, and hardlinks walked straight past them, while the readers that only computed hashes had no cap at all. The second round's fixes have not been reviewed independently again yet, and the README says so.

Write the residual risks down. Some findings were narrowed rather than closed: the unkeyed audit chain, best-effort secret redaction, one egress allowlist shared by setup and executors. The threat model lists what remains with what to do about it, and the README's feature matrix says which protections were verified against a real server and which only with stand-ins. A security claim you cannot point at a test or a measurement is just a claim.

The next post in this series is about the part of the attack surface that talks to models directly: the MCP server.
